intro: Ask the time, give the time, and say when a class, a film or a train starts. You need this every day.
objectifs: Ask the time politely (What time is it? / What's the time?).
Give the time in two ways: with past and to (half past seven) and the digital way (seven thirty).
Show morning or evening with a.m., p.m., in the morning, in the evening.
Say when something happens with “at” (The film starts at eight).

texte: To ask the time, say “What time is it?” or “What's the time?” (very common in British English). With a stranger, be more polite: “Excuse me, do you have the time?” or “Have you got the time?”.
To answer, always start with “It's”. The subject “it” is necessary, like for the weather (lesson 1). Never say “It's seven hours”: we don't use “hours” to give the time.
Use “o'clock” only for exact hours: “It's seven o'clock.” Never use it with minutes.
exemples: What time is it? — It's three o'clock.
Excuse me, have you got the time? — Yes, it's ten past four.
sections.note: “Do you have the time?” (with the) = What time is it? Without “the”, “Do you have time?” means “Are you free? Can you do something?”.

sections.titre: The traditional way: past and to
texte: Say the minutes first, then the hour. From 1 to 30 minutes, use “past” (after the hour). From 31 to 59 minutes, count the minutes before the next hour and use “to”.
15 minutes = “a quarter”, 30 minutes = “half”. We say “a quarter past”, “a quarter to”, but “half past” (never “a half past”).
When the minutes are not 5, 10, 15 and so on, add the word “minutes”: “It's twenty-two minutes past six.”
sections.note: Careful: with “to”, you say the NEXT hour. 7:45 = a quarter to EIGHT. In American English you also hear “a quarter after seven” (7:15) and “a quarter of eight” (7:45).

sections.titre: The digital way: read the numbers
texte: You can also say the hour and then the minutes, like on a screen. It is easy and very common. We always use it for train, plane and appointment times.
For 01 to 09 minutes, say “oh” for the zero: 9:05 = “nine oh five”.
In informal British English, people also say “half seven”. It means 7:30 (half past seven), never 6:30.
exemples: The train leaves at eighteen twenty.

texte: In conversation, English speakers mostly use the 12-hour clock. To be clear, they add “a.m.” (from midnight to midday) or “p.m.” (from midday to midnight), or “in the morning”, “in the afternoon”, “in the evening”, “at night”.
Don't say “It's 14 p.m.”: with a.m. and p.m., use only the numbers 1 to 12. Don't use “o'clock” with a.m. or p.m. either: say “2 p.m.” or “two o'clock in the afternoon”.

lignes: half past seven in the evening

exemples: I finish work at six in the evening.

texte: To say when something happens, use “at” before the time (lesson 18): “at seven”, “at half past six”. The question is “What time…?”: “What time does the film start?”.
For a period: “from nine to five”. For a time that is not exact: “at about eight” or “around eight”.
Three useful expressions: “early” (before the right time), “late” (after the right time), “on time” (at the right time).
exemples: What time does the film start? — At a quarter past eight.
I work from nine to five.
The bus is never on time.
sections.note: Don't say “At what hour…?”. Say “What time…?”.

formule: It's + time: seven o'clock · ten past seven · half past seven · a quarter to eight · seven forty-five
prononciation: “o'clock” is /əˈklɒk/: the first o is weak, the stress is on “clock”.
In “half” /hɑːf/, you don't say the l. The same in “calm” and “walk”.
“quarter” /ˈkwɔːtə/: there is a w sound after the k (kwo-). In British English you don't say the final r.
Stress: thirTEEN (13) but THIRty (30), fifTEEN but FIFty. A mistake here can make you miss a train!
“past” /pɑːst/ and “to” /tə/ are quick and weak: “ten past four” sounds like “ten pas four”.
erreurs: Don't use “hours” to give the time; use “o'clock” for exact hours.
Minutes first, then “to” + the next hour.
Use “o'clock” only with exact hours, never with minutes.
At what hour does it start?
With a.m. / p.m., count from 1 to 12.

dialogue.contexte: At Brussels-South station, Lucie asks a traveller the time and looks for her train.
lignes: Excuse me, have you got the time?
A polite way to ask the time.
Thanks. What time is the next train to Paris?
Let me see… at five fifteen, from platform 3.
A quarter past five? Great, I'm early!
The same time, the traditional way.
Yes, but this train is often late.
Oh no. My meeting is at eight p.m.
Don't worry. It's only one hour and twenty minutes to Paris.

mots: thirty minutes; one of two equal parts
The bus comes in five minutes.
The film is two hours long.
We're early. The shop isn't open.
before the usual or right time
after the usual or right time
The train is on time today.
at the right time, not late

exercices.consigne: Write the time in words with o'clock, past or to.
Write the time like you read it on a screen.
Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: It's half past eight. (or: It's eight thirty.)
What time is it? / What's the time?
The class starts on nine o'clock.
The class starts at nine o'clock.

exercices.consigne: Write the time with a.m. or p.m., or with in the morning / afternoon / evening.
items: 2 p.m. / two o'clock in the afternoon
9.30 p.m. / half past nine in the evening
8.15 a.m. / a quarter past eight in the morning

exercices.consigne: Describe your day in four sentences with times: when you get up, when you start and finish work or classes, when you go to bed.
items: I get up at half past six. I start work at eight o'clock. I finish at a quarter to five. I go to bed at about eleven p.m.

a_retenir: Question: What time is it? / What's the time? Answer: It's… (you need the subject “it”).
Minutes first: ten past seven (7:05 to 7:30), twenty to eight (7:31 to 7:59); a quarter, half past.
Use “o'clock” only for exact hours; never “hours” to give the time.
Digital way: seven thirty, nine oh five; a.m. before midday, p.m. after midday (1 to 12).
When? → What time…? → at eight, at half past six.
